newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan recovery signpost fails to impress markets.
newsitem.headline: Japan recovery signpost fails to impress markets.

text.p: Japan held up a signpost to economic recovery on Tuesday but it was instantly knocked askew by jittery investors who refuse to believe things will get better next year.
Their selloff in the stock market sent Tokyo shares sliding to a 12-month low, with worries about the economy also lifting the dollar against the yen.

Brokers said the stock market shrugged off an announcement by the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) that the diffusion index of leading economic indicators stayed above the "boom or bust" 50 percent line in October for a second straight month.
"We have taken half a step forward in our evaluation of the economy in the October report," an EPA official told reporters.
But market participants said lingering gloom on the economic outlook dampened investors' reaction, and fears remain that foreign investors may pull money out of Japanese assets.
The index of leading indicators stood at 83.3 on a scale of 100 in October. A figure above 50 is taken as suggesting the economy will expand in the coming months.

In the first half of the year, the EPA kept saying that "the basic trend" of the economy was one of recovery. This was partly because some indicators showed weakness in the economy. But the October report dropped that phrase.
Financial markets ignored the data, however, with the key Nikkei average of 225 leading shares losing a hefty 528.75 points or 2.69 percent to close at a 12-month low of 19,161.71.

The dollar rose against the yen in late Tokyo, lifted by the fall in Tokyo stocks, to clear a 114.50 yen resistance point in face of persistent sales of interest by Japanese exporters and profit-takers.
"Today's stock market move and the data correctly show how the Japanese economy is now, and how it will be next year," said Shuji Shirota, a Yamaichi Research Institute economist.

The recovery is at present supported by rising exports, especially of cars to the United States, and buying by consumers to beat a rise in the consumption tax on April 1, the start of fiscal 1997/98, economists said.
Private and government economists say the rise in the tax to five percent from three percent is likely to dampen consumption in the first half of 1997/98.
Last week, the government announced that it expects Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) to grow around 1.9 percent in 1997/98 -- the lowest official forecast in four decades.

"Economic growth may slow in the first half of 1997/98 due to a rise in the consumption tax, but Japan can achieve a sustainable recovery in the whole fiscal year," EPA Minister Taro Aso told reporters last week.
Other data released on Tuesday also showed a healthy economy in the October-December period.

Japan's domestic vehicle production in November rose 8.2 percent from a year earlier to 932,241 vehicles, the third successive month in which output was up year-on-year, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers' Association said.

Meanwhile, the Japan Department Stores' Association said sales at department stores rose 1.1 percent in November from a year earlier to 744.03 billion yen ($6.52 billion) up for the fourth consecutive month on a year-on-year basis. ($1=114 yen)
